name: Modern History
topics: Peace and conflict: Conflict in Europe 1935–1945
Change: Civil rights in the USA 1945–1968
note: Built around Power and Authority 1919–1946, Japan 1904–1937, Conflict in Europe 1935–1945 and Civil Rights in the USA 1945–1968 (2017 syllabus, used for HSC 2027). Check the options your school studies.

cards.f: Define totalitarianism.
cards.b: A system where one party and leader control every part of public and private life through ideology, propaganda, terror and control of the economy and media.

cards.f: Key terms of the Treaty of Versailles (1919) for Germany.
cards.b: War guilt clause (Article 231), reparations (set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921), army limited to 100 000, no air force, Rhineland demilitarised, loss of territory and all colonies.

cards.f: Why was the Weimar Republic weak from the start?
cards.b: Blamed for Versailles (the 'stab in the back' myth), proportional representation gave unstable coalitions, Article 48 emergency powers, and attacks from the left (Spartacists) and right (Kapp Putsch).

cards.f: What was the hyperinflation crisis of 1923?
cards.b: After Germany missed reparations, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr. The government printed money to pay striking workers and the mark collapsed, wiping out savings.

cards.f: What was the Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch?
cards.b: Hitler's failed attempt to seize power in Bavaria in November 1923. In prison he wrote Mein Kampf and decided to gain power legally through elections.

cards.f: How did the Great Depression help the Nazis?
cards.b: US loans were recalled, unemployment reached about 6 million by 1932, and desperate voters turned to extremes. Nazi seats rose from 12 (1928) to 230 (July 1932).

cards.f: How did Hitler become Chancellor?
cards.b: Not by winning a majority: conservative elites led by von Papen persuaded Hindenburg to appoint him on 30 January 1933, believing they could control him.

cards.f: Significance of the Reichstag Fire (February 1933).
cards.b: Blamed on the communists. The Reichstag Fire Decree suspended civil liberties and allowed mass arrests of opponents.

cards.f: What did the Enabling Act (March 1933) do?
cards.b: Gave Hitler's cabinet power to make laws without the Reichstag for four years, the legal basis of the dictatorship.

cards.f: What was Gleichschaltung?
cards.b: 'Coordination': bringing every part of German society under Nazi control. Trade unions were abolished, other parties banned, and state governments taken over in 1933.

cards.f: Night of the Long Knives (June 1934): what and why?
cards.b: Hitler had Röhm and other SA leaders and opponents killed to remove a rival power and win the army's support. After Hindenburg died in August, Hitler became Führer and the army swore an oath to him.

cards.f: Role of propaganda in Nazi Germany.
cards.b: Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda controlled press, radio, film (Triumph of the Will) and rallies to build the Führer myth and spread Nazi ideology.

cards.f: Role of terror in Nazi Germany.
cards.b: The SS (Himmler) and Gestapo used surveillance, informers, arrest without trial and concentration camps such as Dachau (1933) to crush opposition.

cards.f: What were the Nuremberg Laws (1935)?
cards.b: Laws that took German citizenship from Jews and banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and other Germans.

cards.f: What was Kristallnacht?
cards.b: The 'Night of Broken Glass', 9 to 10 November 1938: a state-organised attack on Jewish shops, homes and synagogues, with about 30 000 Jewish men sent to camps.

cards.f: How did Mussolini come to power?
cards.b: Fascist squads used violence against socialists; after the March on Rome in October 1922, King Victor Emmanuel III appointed him prime minister.

cards.f: How did Mussolini build his dictatorship?
cards.b: The Acerbo Law (1923) gave the largest party two-thirds of seats, the murder of Matteotti (1924) silenced opposition, and by 1926 other parties were banned.

cards.f: What were the Lateran Pacts (1929)?
cards.b: Agreements between Mussolini and the Pope recognising Vatican City and making Catholicism the state religion, winning Church support.

cards.f: How did Stalin consolidate power after Lenin?
cards.b: As General Secretary he controlled appointments, then defeated Trotsky, then Zinoviev and Kamenev, then Bukharin, using 'Socialism in One Country'.

cards.f: Stalin's Five-Year Plans.
cards.b: From 1928, state targets for rapid industrial growth (coal, steel, electricity). Output rose sharply at great human cost, including forced labour in the Gulag.

cards.f: What was collectivisation and its result?
cards.b: Forcing peasants into collective farms from 1929. Kulaks were deported or killed, and famine followed, including the Holodomor in Ukraine (1932–33).

cards.f: What were the Great Purges?
cards.b: Stalin's terror of 1936–38: show trials of old Bolsheviks, purges of the army and party, and about 750 000 executions by the NKVD.

cards.f: Why did the League of Nations fail in the 1930s?
cards.b: No army, the US never joined, it needed unanimous decisions, and it failed to stop Japan in Manchuria (1931) and Italy in Abyssinia (1935).

cards.f: What did fascist and communist regimes have in common?
cards.b: One-party rule, a cult of the leader, propaganda, terror and secret police, control of the economy and youth, and rejection of liberal democracy.

cards.f: What was the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) and its result?
cards.b: War over influence in Korea and Manchuria. Japan won (Tsushima naval battle, 1905), and the Treaty of Portsmouth gave it Port Arthur, southern Sakhalin and control of Korea: the first Asian victory over a European power.

cards.f: When did Japan annex Korea?
cards.b: 1910, after making it a protectorate in 1905.

cards.f: Who held power under the Meiji Constitution of 1889?
cards.b: Sovereignty belonged to the Emperor. The cabinet, military and genro (elder statesmen) held real power; the Diet had limited powers and the army and navy answered to the Emperor.

cards.f: What were the Twenty-One Demands (1915)?
cards.b: Japanese demands on China during World War I for economic and political rights. They caused Chinese anger and Western suspicion.

cards.f: What was 'Taisho democracy'?
cards.b: The 1910s and 1920s, when party cabinets, a growing middle class and new ideas gave Japan more democratic politics, e.g. Hara Takashi, the first commoner prime minister (1918).

cards.f: What did the Washington Naval Conference (1921–22) mean for Japan?
cards.b: A 5:5:3 capital ship ratio for the US, Britain and Japan. Many in the navy saw it as humiliating, and the Anglo-Japanese Alliance ended.

cards.f: Effects of the Great Kanto Earthquake (1923).
cards.b: Over 100 000 dead and Tokyo and Yokohama destroyed. Koreans were murdered in the panic, and the costs weakened the economy.

cards.f: What two laws of 1925 show the contradictions of the period?
cards.b: The General Election Law gave all men over 25 the vote, while the Peace Preservation Law made it a crime to oppose the imperial system or private property.

cards.f: What were the zaibatsu?
cards.b: Large family-run business conglomerates such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi with close ties to political parties, resented as corrupt during the Depression.

cards.f: How did the Great Depression affect Japan?
cards.b: Silk exports to the US collapsed, rural poverty deepened, and anger at parties and zaibatsu grew support for the military and expansion.

cards.f: Why was the London Naval Treaty (1930) so controversial?
cards.b: It accepted limits on Japan's navy against naval objections, sparking claims the government had violated the Emperor's command of the military. PM Hamaguchi was shot later that year.

cards.f: What was the Mukden (Manchurian) Incident?
cards.b: On 18 September 1931 Kwantung Army officers blew up part of the South Manchurian Railway, blamed China, and used it as an excuse to occupy Manchuria without government approval.

cards.f: What was Manchukuo?
cards.b: The puppet state Japan created in Manchuria in 1932, with the last Qing emperor Puyi as its nominal ruler.

cards.f: Japan and the League of Nations.
cards.b: The Lytton Report condemned Japan over Manchuria, and Japan left the League in 1933.

cards.f: What was the May 15 Incident (1932)?
cards.b: Young naval officers assassinated Prime Minister Inukai. It ended party cabinets until after the war.

cards.f: What was the February 26 Incident (1936)?
cards.b: An attempted coup by young Imperial Way (Kodoha) army officers in Tokyo who killed several ministers. The Emperor had it put down, and the Control (Toseiha) faction gained power.

cards.f: What was the Anti-Comintern Pact (1936)?
cards.b: An agreement between Japan and Nazi Germany against international communism (the Soviet Union). Italy joined in 1937.

cards.f: What was the Marco Polo Bridge Incident?
cards.b: A clash between Japanese and Chinese troops near Beijing on 7 July 1937 that grew into full-scale war with China.

cards.f: Why did militarism grow in Japan in the 1930s?
cards.b: Depression hardship, distrust of corrupt parties, ultranationalist societies, army independence under the constitution, and fear of communism and the West.

cards.f: Why did Italy invade Abyssinia (1935) and what did it show?
cards.b: Mussolini wanted an empire and revenge for Adwa (1896). Weak League sanctions (no oil ban) showed the League could not stop aggression.

cards.f: Remilitarisation of the Rhineland (March 1936).
cards.b: Hitler sent troops into the demilitarised Rhineland, breaking Versailles and Locarno. Britain and France did nothing.

cards.f: Why was the Spanish Civil War (1936–39) significant?
cards.b: Germany and Italy helped Franco and tested weapons (the bombing of Guernica, 1937); the USSR helped the Republic; Britain and France stayed out.

cards.f: What was the Anschluss?
cards.b: Germany's union with Austria in March 1938, forbidden by Versailles.

cards.f: What was agreed at Munich (September 1938)?
cards.b: Britain, France and Italy let Germany take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia. Chamberlain claimed 'peace for our time'.

cards.f: When did appeasement end?
cards.b: After Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. Britain and France then guaranteed Poland.

cards.f: What was the Nazi-Soviet Pact (August 1939)?
cards.b: A non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Poland and Eastern Europe. It freed Hitler to attack Poland without a two-front war.

cards.f: When and how did the war in Europe start?
cards.b: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

cards.f: What was Blitzkrieg?
cards.b: 'Lightning war': fast attacks combining tanks, motorised infantry and dive bombers to break through and encircle the enemy.

cards.f: Fall of France (1940): key events.
cards.b: Germany attacked through the Ardennes in May, the British evacuated about 338 000 troops from Dunkirk, and France signed an armistice in June. Southern France became the Vichy regime.

cards.f: Why did Germany lose the Battle of Britain (1940)?
cards.b: Radar, the RAF's organisation and fighter production, and the Luftwaffe's switch from airfields to bombing cities (the Blitz). Invasion was postponed.

cards.f: What was Operation Barbarossa?
cards.b: The German invasion of the USSR on 22 June 1941. It reached Moscow but stalled in the winter, and the Soviet counter-offensive pushed it back.

cards.f: Why was Stalingrad a turning point?
cards.b: Germany's 6th Army surrendered in February 1943 after encirclement, its first huge defeat. The initiative passed to the Red Army.

cards.f: What was the significance of the Battle of Kursk (July 1943)?
cards.b: The largest tank battle in history. Germany's last major offensive in the east failed, and the Soviets advanced from then on.

cards.f: Significance of El Alamein (1942).
cards.b: Montgomery's victory in Egypt stopped Rommel's advance in North Africa and led to the Axis being driven out of Africa by May 1943.

cards.f: What was D-Day?
cards.b: The Allied invasion of Normandy on 6 June 1944 (Operation Overlord). It opened a second front in the west.

cards.f: What was decided at Yalta (February 1945)?
cards.b: Germany would be divided into zones, Poland's borders moved, free elections promised in Eastern Europe, and the USSR would join the war against Japan.

cards.f: When did the war in Europe end?
cards.b: Germany surrendered unconditionally on 7 to 8 May 1945 (VE Day), after Hitler's suicide on 30 April.

cards.f: What was the Wannsee Conference?
cards.b: A meeting of Nazi officials in January 1942 to coordinate the 'Final Solution': the systematic murder of Europe's Jews.

cards.f: What were the Einsatzgruppen?
cards.b: SS mobile killing squads that followed the army into the USSR and shot over a million Jews and others, e.g. Babi Yar (1941).

cards.f: Collaboration and resistance in occupied Europe.
cards.b: Some cooperated (Vichy France, Quisling in Norway); others resisted through sabotage, partisan war, hiding Jews and intelligence (French Resistance, Polish Home Army).

cards.f: Why is the Allied bombing of Germany debated?
cards.b: It damaged industry and tied down German forces, but cities such as Hamburg (1943) and Dresden (1945) suffered huge civilian deaths.

cards.f: Why did Germany lose the war?
cards.b: Fighting on several fronts, the USSR's huge manpower and production, US entry (December 1941), Allied air and sea power, and Hitler's strategic mistakes.

cards.f: What were the Jim Crow laws?
cards.b: State and local laws in the South that enforced racial segregation in schools, transport and public places, backed by Plessy v Ferguson (1896)'s 'separate but equal'.

cards.f: How did World War II change the civil rights movement?
cards.b: Over a million African Americans served abroad while facing segregation at home ('Double V' campaign), and the NAACP's membership grew rapidly.

cards.f: What did Truman's Executive Order 9981 (1948) do?
cards.b: It ordered equal treatment in the armed forces, leading to their desegregation.

cards.f: Brown v Board of Education (1954).
cards.b: The Supreme Court ruled segregated public schools unconstitutional, overturning 'separate but equal' in education. Thurgood Marshall argued it for the NAACP.

cards.f: Why did Emmett Till's murder (1955) matter?
cards.b: A 14-year-old Black boy was murdered in Mississippi, and his killers were acquitted. His mother's open-casket funeral shocked the nation and spurred activism.

cards.f: Montgomery Bus Boycott: dates and outcome.
cards.b: December 1955 to December 1956, after Rosa Parks' arrest. The Supreme Court (Browder v Gayle) ruled bus segregation unconstitutional, and Martin Luther King Jr became a national leader.

cards.f: What happened at Little Rock (1957)?
cards.b: Governor Faubus used the National Guard to stop nine Black students entering Central High. Eisenhower sent federal troops to protect them.

cards.f: What was the SCLC?
cards.b: The Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in 1957 and led by King, using churches and nonviolent direct action.

cards.f: What were the Greensboro sit-ins?
cards.b: From February 1960 four Black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter. The tactic spread across the South and led to the founding of SNCC.

cards.f: What were the Freedom Rides (1961)?
cards.b: CORE organised integrated bus trips through the South to test a ruling against segregated interstate bus terminals. Riders were attacked, and a bus was burned in Anniston.

cards.f: Why was the Birmingham campaign (1963) a turning point?
cards.b: Police chief Bull Connor used dogs and fire hoses on children on TV. National outrage pushed Kennedy to propose a civil rights bill; King wrote 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'.

cards.f: March on Washington (August 1963).
cards.b: About 250 000 people marched for jobs and freedom; King gave the 'I Have a Dream' speech.

cards.f: What did the Civil Rights Act 1964 do?
cards.b: Banned segregation in public places and employment discrimination on the basis of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin.

cards.f: What was Freedom Summer (1964)?
cards.b: A campaign to register Black voters in Mississippi. Three workers (Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner) were murdered.

cards.f: What happened at Selma (1965)?
cards.b: On 'Bloody Sunday' (7 March) state troopers beat marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Public outrage helped pass the Voting Rights Act.

cards.f: What did the Voting Rights Act 1965 do?
cards.b: Banned literacy tests and gave federal oversight of voter registration in states with a history of discrimination. Black voter registration rose sharply.

cards.f: Malcolm X's ideas.
cards.b: A Nation of Islam spokesman who criticised nonviolence and integration, urging Black pride, self-defence and separation. He was assassinated in February 1965.

cards.f: What was Black Power?
cards.b: A slogan popularised by Stokely Carmichael in 1966 calling for Black self-reliance, pride and political and economic power.

cards.f: Who were the Black Panthers?
cards.b: A party founded in Oakland in 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale. They ran armed patrols watching the police and community programs such as free breakfasts.

cards.f: Why were there urban riots in the 1960s?
cards.b: Poverty, unemployment, poor housing and police brutality in northern cities, e.g. Watts (1965) and Detroit (1967). The Kerner Report (1968) blamed white racism.

cards.f: What happened on 4 April 1968?
cards.b: Martin Luther King Jr was assassinated in Memphis. Riots followed in many cities, and the Civil Rights Act 1968 (Fair Housing Act) was passed days later.

cards.f: Role of the federal government in civil rights.
cards.b: Mixed: the Supreme Court led on desegregation, presidents acted when forced by crises (Eisenhower at Little Rock, Johnson's legislation), and the FBI under Hoover spied on leaders.
